name: Okodia
confidence_why: Williamson's 1988 study of Ịjọ tone places Okordia among the dialects with two tones plus downstep and her 1994 encyclopedia article says the same of the whole inland Ịjọ group, and nothing disagrees, but both statements are hers alone and the two Port Harcourt phonology theses on Okordia (Ekeoma 1993, Ofuya 1993) were not available.

catalog_quote: West Ịjọ consists first of the inland Ịjọ group, comprising three isolated languages: Biseni, Akịta (Okordia), and Tugbeni (Oruma); and second of Ịzọn, a large language with a complex dialect situation. ... Typically, Ịjọ dialects have vowel harmony with nine oral and nine nasal vowels, though some have reduced the number. Labio velar stops occur in all dialects; in many dialects they are in contrast with voiced implosives. KAKIBA and inland Ịjọ have two tones plus downstep, some Ịzọn dialects have two tones without downstep, while many other Ịzọn dialects and Nembe–Akaha have pitch–accent systems. The typical root structure is CVCV(CV) (where C = Consonant and V = Vowel).
world_status: statement found in an open source

Table 1 on the next page shows the pitch patterns borne in isolation by cognate words of three different tone cl[asses] ... [fn. 1: The dialects are here numbered according to a code in which the first digit indicates the language and the later ones indicate subgrouping within the language. The dialect names are abbreviated as follows: OR = Oruma ... BI = Biseni ... OA = Okordia ...] [Table 1 row: '13 OA HH HH H'H HH ... LL'] ... In terms of the usual typology, dialects 11-12, 312-319 would be classified as two-level tone systems without downstep, dialects 13-311 as two-level tone systems with downstep, and dialects 321-42 as pitch-accent systems.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Okordia (Williamson's the StressTyp2 entry for this language, Inland Ijo group 1x together with 11 Oruma and 12 Biseni) is classed as a two-level (H/L) tone language with downstep, grouped with Eastern Ijo, unlike Oruma and Biseni (two-level, no downstep) and unlike the Izon pitch accent dialects; her Table 1 gives Okordia isolation forms with H'H downstep patterns. No statement about word stress; lexical pitch is tonal.
new_statements.exceptions: Williamson herself doubts the usefulness of the tone vs pitch accent typology for Ijo ('These different characterizations of otherwise closely-related, often mutually intelligible, dialects raise doubts as to the usefulness of this typology') and analyses all dialects with tone classes plus a 'strong syllable' locus; the OA-specific parameters of that analysis could not be recovered from snippets. Jenewari 1989:114 gives a coarser summary (Nkoroo + Eastern Ijo two tones + downstep; Kolokuma/Mein two tones without downstep; 'others' accentual) that does not name Okodia.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical tone on words/morphemes; Table 1 = pitch patterns of cognate words in isolation (citation forms). Williamson's Ijo framework operates on 'tone groups' (word + clitics) within sentences.
new_statements.identity_note: Williamson 1988 labels the lect 'Okordia' (abbreviation OA, dialect code 13), one of three lects of her language 1 (Inland Ijo: 11 Oruma, 12 Biseni, 13 Okordia) = Glottolog okod1238 Okodia / ISO okd (also 'Akita'). Note her classification separates Okordia (downstep) from Biseni bise1238 and Oruma orum1241 (no downstep), so the statement should not be generalised to 'Inland Ijo'.

new_statements.relation_note: Same reading as the existing Williamson 1988 statement (tone language, no stress statement). Note a mild tension with the 1988 snippet reconstruction held by the project: Williamson 1988 puts Oruma and Biseni (dialects 11-12) among the two-level systems WITHOUT downstep and Okordia (13) among those WITH downstep, whereas this 1994 article lumps all of inland Ijo together as 'two tones plus downstep'. Both agree Okordia has two tones with downstep; neither mentions stress. Also confirms the naming identity Okordia = Akita in the inland Ijo group, consistent with the catalog record 'Okodia' (empty rule).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Okordia is placed in 'the inland Ijo group, comprising three isolated languages: Biseni, Akita (Okordia), and Tugbeni (Oruma)' (p. 517), and inland Ijo is characterized as having two tones (H, L) plus downstep. The article says nothing about word stress or any fixed prominence position; the only prosodic statement is the tonal typology, with pitch accent systems attributed to other Ijo varieties (many Izon dialects and Nembe-Akaha), not to inland Ijo.
new_statements.exceptions: none for Okordia; the sentence is a group-level statement covering all three inland Ijo languages, with no Okordia-specific data
new_statements.identity_note: Williamson 1994/2009 names the language 'Akita (Okordia)' as one of the three 'isolated languages' of the inland Ijo group (with Biseni and Tugbeni (Oruma)), p. 517; the tonal statement is made at the level of 'inland Ijo' as a group, not for Okordia alone. Glottolog records both theses under 'Okordia = Okodia [okd]'.

readall_conflicts: No source opened states a word-stress position, so there is no stress conflict. The only disagreement is within the tonal characterization: Williamson 1994/2009 (p. 518) says 'KAKIBA and inland Ijo have two tones plus downstep' for the whole inland group (Biseni, Okordia, Oruma), whereas the earlier Williamson 1988 chapter (per the scanned-snippet reconstruction held by the project) places Okordia (code 13) among the 'two-level tone systems with downstep' but Oruma and Biseni (11-12) among those without downstep. For Okordia itself both agree: two tones with downstep, no stress statement. The two 1993 Port Harcourt MA theses, which are the only Okordia-specific phonologies listed, could not be opened, so whether either treats stress or prominence remains unknown.
